content.title: Systems of Two Linear Equations in Two Variables
content.overview: A system of two linear equations consists of two equations with two variables (usually x and y). The solution is the ordered pair (x, y) that satisfies both equations simultaneously. On the ACT, the most efficient method for solving these is often the Elimination Method.
learning_objectives: Identify the solution to a system as the intersection point of two lines.
Apply the Elimination Method to solve for x and y.
Recognize systems with no solution or infinitely many solutions.
Verify solutions by substituting values back into the original equations.

sections.title: The Elimination Method
sections.content:
The Elimination Method involves manipulating the equations so that adding or subtracting them cancels out one variable, leaving a single-variable equation. First, choose a variable to eliminate. Multiply one or both equations by constants so that the coefficients of that variable have the same magnitude. If the coefficients have opposite signs (e.g., 5 and -5), add the equations. If they have the same sign (e.g., 5 and 5), subtract the equations. Once one variable is found, substitute it back into either original equation to find the second variable.

![A flowchart showing the steps: Match Coefficients, Add or Subtract, Solve for One, Back-Substitute, and Verify.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/2f97727e-8ae8-4cb1-a2f2-fe41bb0e4b8e-1786505624473-340.webp)

sections.title: Types of Solutions
sections.content: Most ACT systems have exactly one solution, representing the point where two lines intersect. However, two special cases exist: 1) No Solution occurs when the lines are parallel (same slope, different y-intercepts); algebraically, the variables cancel out and leave a false statement like 0 = 5. 2) Infinitely Many Solutions occur when the equations represent the same line; algebraically, the variables cancel out and leave a true statement like 0 = 0.

worked_examples.question:
Solve the system of equations for (x, y): 
3x + 2y = 16 
7x + y = 19
worked_examples.solution:
Step 1: Choose a variable to eliminate. It is easiest to eliminate y by multiplying the second equation by -2. 
Step 2: Rewrite the equations. 
Eq 1: 3x + 2y = 16 
Eq 2 (multiplied): -14x - 2y = -38 
Step 3: Add the equations together. (3x - 14x) + (2y - 2y) = (16 - 38) results in -11x = -22. 
Step 4: Solve for x. x = 2. 
Step 5: Substitute x = 2 into the original second equation: 7(2) + y = 19 -> 14 + y = 19 -> y = 5. 
Step 6: The solution is (2, 5).

common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply the constant on the right side of the equals sign when scaling an equation.
Subtracting equations incorrectly when signs are negative (e.g., -3y minus -3y is 0, not -6y).
Swapping the x and y values in the final ordered pair (x, y).
Only solving for one variable and stopping before finding the second.
exam_tips: If the equations are already solved for one variable (e.g., y = 2x + 3), use Substitution instead of Elimination.
Always perform a 'Final Check' by plugging your (x, y) answer into the equation you did NOT use for back-substitution.
If the question asks for the value of x + y, you don't always need to solve for them individually; look for a way to add the equations directly.
content.recap: To solve a system of two linear equations, use the Elimination Method to remove one variable, solve for the other, and then back-substitute. A solution is the point where the two lines intersect on a coordinate plane.

knowledge_claims.content: A solution to a system of two linear equations is an ordered pair (x, y) that makes both equations true simultaneously.
Graphically, the solution to a system of two linear equations represents the point of intersection of the two lines.
The first step in the Elimination Method is to multiply one or both equations by constants so that the coefficients of one variable match in magnitude.
When using elimination, add the equations if the target variable's coefficients have opposite signs, and subtract if they have the same sign.
After solving for one variable in a system, substitute that value back into either original equation to solve for the remaining variable.
To verify a solution (x, y), the values must be plugged into both original equations to ensure they satisfy both.
A system has no solution if the two lines are parallel, meaning they have the same slope but different y-intercepts.
A system has infinitely many solutions if the two equations represent the same line.
If the variables in a system cancel out and leave a false statement (like 0 = 7), the system has no solution.
If the variables in a system cancel out and leave a true statement (like 0 = 0), the system has infinitely many solutions.
A common error is failing to multiply the constant term on the right side of the equation when scaling for elimination.
Substitution is often faster than elimination if one equation is already isolated for a single variable (e.g., x = 3y - 4).

items.stem:
What ordered pair (x, y) solves the system x + y = 11 and 2x − y = 7?
A) (5, 6)
B) (7, 4)
C) (6, 5)
D) (4, 7)
items.explanation: Eliminating one variable and substituting back gives x = 6 and y = 5.

items.stem:
What ordered pair (x, y) solves the system 2x + y = 4 and x − y = 5?
A) (-2, 3)
B) (4, -3)
C) (3, −2)
D) (1, 0)
items.explanation: Eliminating one variable and substituting back gives x = 3 and y = -2.

videoLesson.title: Eliminate One Variable Using Multiplication
videoLesson.description: You will recognize which variable's coefficients can be matched and eliminated. Multiply to match coefficients, add or subtract to remove that variable, then substitute to find the other.
